segments.text: Welcome to People Behind the Science. You're listening to episode number 462 featuring our
guest researcher, Dr. Mike Levin. Now today, listeners, we're going to get an inside look
at the life of another phenomenal scientist. And this episode was made possible by listeners like
you. So a big thank you to everyone who's helped us keep this program going through contributions
to our crowdfunding Patreon campaign at patreon.com slash science podcast. Now, if you're able to
dedicate $1 or more to help us continue sharing fantastic stories from scientists, we would
really appreciate it. And we'll give you a shout out on an upcoming episode. Now today, you are going
to hear some fantastic stories from Mike's life in science. So get ready to meet another one of our
brilliant people behind the science. Every day discoveries are made that will change our
understanding of the world around us. Dr. Marie McNeely is here to bring you the brilliant minds
who are making these discoveries so they can share their incredible stories and take you on an
amazing journey. Welcome to People Behind the Science.
Good one and welcome to the People Behind the Science podcast. Today, I am delighted to introduce
you all to our guest today, Dr. Michael Levin. So Mike, welcome to our show. How are you?
Thank you very much. I'm very happy to be here. I'm fine.
Well, we are happy to have you with us and excited to learn more about you and the work that you do.
So listeners, let me take a moment to tell you a little bit about Mike.
Mike is a professor and Vannevar Bush Endowed Chair in the Department of Biology at Tufts
University. He's also Director of the Allen Discovery Center at Tufts and Director of the
Tufts Center for Regenerative and Developmental Biology. In addition, Mike is a visiting scholar
at the Wyss Institute at Harvard, and he received his Bachelor's Degree in Computer Science and Biology
from Tufts University and was awarded his PhD in Genetics from Harvard University Medical School.
Mike then remained at Harvard University afterwards to conduct postdoctoral research in molecular
embryology under a Helen Hay Whitney Foundation postdoctoral fellowship. In his next career step,
Mike joined the faculty at Harvard, and he also became a member of the research staff at the
Forsyth Institute. During his career, Mike has received numerous honors and accolades.
He was awarded a Junior Investigator Award from the Society for Physical Regulation in Biology and
Medicine, the Distinguished Scholar Award from Tufts University, the Scientist of Vision Award from the
International Functional Electrical Stimulation Society, and the Established Investigator Award from the
American Heart Association. In our interview today, Mike is going to share more about both his life and
his science. So Mike, we want to get to know you both as a scientist, but also as a person. So can
you start by giving us some insight into how you spend your time when you're not busy doing science?
Well, there's not a tremendous amount of time in which I'm not busy doing science, but during that
time, it's mostly spent with my family. I like to be outdoors, I kayak, I take lots of pictures,
nature photography, that sort of thing. But basically, if I'm not with my kids and my wife,
I am doing science.
Awesome. So how'd you get into photography?
Well, I'm outside a lot. I live near the ocean and I kayak, as I said, and I like to take both
panoramic shots, but also a lot of micro photography. So I take a lot of pictures of
insects and various weird small things that I find as I'm walking around.
Very cool. Great to hear a little bit about what occupies your time when you're not hard at work.
But I do want to chat about your work next. I know you have so many cool projects going on.
How do you describe what you do to someone who's not familiar with your research specifically or
with your field?
Generally speaking, what I like to do is to think very deeply about how living things work. And this
is broadly in terms of how cells and tissues make decisions, computations that might happen
in living media, the mechanisms by which cells and larger structures arise during evolution and how
they work in the organism. So my job, I think, is to figure out how to ask nature various questions
about how these things work and to get new ideas and to test whether our existing ideas are useful.
Very cool. Well, great description. And I look forward to jumping into more detail on the specific
projects as we go through our conversation today. But I do want to take a moment to talk about what
motivates you. I think as a scientist, you spend so much time in your research and doing the work
that it can be hard to get motivation sometimes. And I'm always on the lookout for
motivation and inspiration in my own life. So Mike, do you have a favorite quote or a saying
that really resonates with you? I do. And I agree with you. I think that this sort of
motivation is very important. One of the things that we see a lot in education, let's say for our
grad students, is an emphasis on being rigorous in terms of disproving ideas and ruling out hypotheses
and things like this. And those are, of course, an essential part of science. But I think another
essential component is being able to get inspiration to get good ideas in the first place. And certainly,
this is something that I talk to my students about a lot, is the flip side of this. Before,
you can test and rule out your ideas, it's good to be able to get good ideas in the first place.
So I think that's an important area. In terms of motivational quotes, there are many. Some of
them are on my Twitter feed. I like to put those up. But there's one in particular that I was thinking
of last night, and I'll read it to you. This is by Lauren Isley, who's an American anthropologist
and science writer. He writes,
While I was sitting one night with a poet friend, watching a great opera performed in a tent under arc
lights, the poet took my arm and pointed silently. Far up, blundering out of the night,
a huge cecropia moth swept past from light to light over the posturings of the actors.
He doesn't know, my friend whispered excited. He's passing through an alien universe, brightly lit,
but invisible to him. He's in another play, and he doesn't see us. He doesn't know. Maybe it's
happening right now to us. That's the quote. I like it a lot because I think that what you can get
from this is the idea that every living system, including us, lives in a certain world where it can
perceive some set of signals and from this build sort of model or an understanding of the world
around it. But these models are fundamentally incomplete, and there's lots of interesting
things going on that we are completely oblivious of until we ask the right questions to be able
to probe. And there are worlds all around us in terms of other aspects of the electromagnetic
spectrum and different forces that we don't feel. And to me, I think one of the most exciting parts
of science and the work we do is to get a glimpse of some of these other worlds that we're immersed
in but don't necessarily know about. I love that. Well, fantastic quote. And I love that you brought
up this idea of the importance of getting good ideas for science. I think this is something that
worries or plagues young scientists. They're worried that they're not going to be able to think about
good ideas or that they'll run out of good ideas. So how do you come up with the ideas that you
pursue in science? There are two components to this. So getting ideas, I think, comes from reading and
thinking broadly. So the kinds of things that I read on a weekly basis range from computer science
and physics and cognitive science and all sorts of other fields quite outside or at least traditionally
thought to be outside of the sort of biology I'm supposed to be doing in my day job. And I think
reading and talking to people and thinking very broadly really helps get ideas that are new and
have not yet been explored and thought about in terms of getting good ideas. The next step,
of course, is knowing whether any of them are any good to the extent that you should be putting
in effort to following them up. And this really just comes from experience in honing one's intuition.
And this is something else that I work on with my students is to have the ability to develop a sort
of nose for things that seem like they're deep and profound and maybe useful and testable, even when
these ideas are not necessarily something that everybody else is going to immediately recognize
as a good idea. So over your scientific career, practicing following that sense of where the
important discoveries might be and learning to develop a little bit of resistance to the status
quo when they might be telling you that this is not anything that's worthwhile and ultimately just
really developing your own sense of being able to recognize when these things are in front of you.
So I think it's a combination of those two things.
And I think absolutely I agree with the idea of reading outside your field and reading broadly
because you're able to make connections that a lot of people in your field who are sort of having
only that narrow focus won't ever think of because they're not being exposed to these different
areas and ideas. So great to hear about what motivates and inspires you, Mike. But I want
to hear a little bit more next about some of the people who might have motivated or inspired you
along your path as a scientist. So do you have particular mentors or inspirational figures that
you can really point to who had a big impact?
There have been many. So in terms of people I've actually worked with, of course, starting with
Susan Ernst, who is a professor here at Tufts University when I was an undergraduate here.
She was the first person I did formal research with and she was very influential for me.
And then my PhD advisor, Cliff Tabin, and my postdoc mentor, Mark Mercola, all of these people were
personal mentors to me. But in terms of scientific inspiration and more broadly in the field,
there are numerous in effect in our lab here at the Allen Center at Tufts. We have a whole set of
portraits in the main hall called our Wall of Heroes, which are basically pictures of people
who have inspired the work that we do here. I figured I'd pick one that we can just talk about.
One of my all-time favorites is a guy by the name of Alexander Gurevich. And he lived at the early
part of the last century and he discovered mitogenetic radiation, otherwise known as ultra-weak
photon emission from living systems. He was the first person to talk about morphogenetic fields.
He was very influential in applying mathematical principles to understand cell
biology and this idea of field concepts and mathematical descriptions of large-scale
structures during embryonic development. He was one of the founders, really, of quantitative biology.
And he did some very, very impressive things that have always inspired me. And a lot of this was
done under basically starvation conditions in Russia and various parts of Eastern Europe during
wartime. So he was incredibly inspiring, both because of his vision. He was very much ahead of his time
in a lot of the things he did, but also just in terms of the personal perseverance and the
dedication to science in the middle of fairly unbelievable conditions in which you try to
make progress on science.
I think it puts it all into perspective when you think about the problems you're facing in
your science and your life today, right?
Yeah, exactly.
Well, wonderful to hear about some of these people who inspired you over the course of your
career. And I love this idea of a wall of heroes. Is that something you came up with?
Yes, I believe I did. It's just literally a set of portraits that we had printed out
and little plaques underneath them to remind us of who they are and what they did. And
they're very unusual people. So these are not necessarily the obvious Charles Darwin.
Einstein. Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, it's not that. A set of people that a lot of folks have probably never heard of.
Well, I think that is so cool. And I'm curious to hear a little bit more next, Mike, about
how you first got interested in science and maybe particularly this area of science. So
do you have some early memories of when this curiosity first got sparked for you that you can share
with us today?
So I was born in Moscow, Russia. And when I was about four or five years old, we had one
of those ancient TV sets with the vacuum tubes in it. The screen was tiny, but the thing itself
was massive. And my dad used to take the back panel off of this giant TV set and let me look
at all the components that were inside. And I remember just being absolutely struck by the fact
that somebody actually knew how to put all that stuff in there in exactly the right combination
to get the effect we want, which is to be able to watch cartoons off the other side.
And it just seemed like whoever that was and however it is that they figured out exactly
how to put that stuff in, that seemed to me like the most important thing in the world,
that if there was some way of figuring these things out, that just had to be incredible.
And then shortly thereafter, I met this older kid who was into collecting insects. And we went
around outside and collected caterpillars and beetles and things like this. And I think that was the
beginnings of my thinking about what's inside of those things, analogous to what's inside the TV
and how did they get to be where they are. And of course, they're far more impressive than any of
the actual technology that we had is what these living things were doing. And I think between those
things together, it sort of cemented for me this idea that I would like to understand living things
from an almost engineering perspective in terms of how they're put together and how we might
reconfigure that for a better understanding of what's going on.
Gotcha. So then can you tell us what were some of these key steps or key moments from when you
were an early kid starting to get curious about biology and science and how things come together?
And what took you from that point to where you are today, now a professor at Tufts?
Well, basic steps. I was very much into computers and this was the early 80s and kind of the heyday of
people being able to do things with computers in their home and hacking and so on.
And I learned the program and I was actually writing software for money even before I got
to high school. And then throughout high school, basically, the idea was that I was going to go
to college for a degree in computer science. The idea being that I would then eventually work
in artificial intelligence and make robots that repair themselves and those kind of things.
And while I was in college and I was an undergrad at Tufts in computer science, I had a software
company with my dad actually at that time.
Oh, that's cool.
Eventually, it became pretty clear that in order to make the kind of impact in that field
that I wanted to make, I would have to learn from the natural world. It just didn't seem
like there was enough going on in computer engineering and artificial intelligence to
enable us to really make profound progress without understanding how the living world did
it. And so I got a second major in biology at Tufts. And then shortly after that, I gave up
the software company and went to graduate school for my PhD in biology. And the idea was to
simply learn what we knew about how embryogenesis work, how complex organisms assemble themselves
with no external inputs. Every cell knows what to do to cooperate with other cells to make
a complicated body plan. So these are the things that I wanted to learn. So I did that for four
years. I got my PhD and then I did a postdoc also for four years in a different lab at Harvard
Medical School. And then after that, I got my first independent position at a place called
Foresight Institute, which was on the Harvard Medical School campus. During all that time,
I was working in fairly traditional molecular cell biology and genetics because the goal was to
really learn what went on in that field. But in the back of my head, I was always interested in
a pretty weird topic that I first sort of formulated around 1986 or 7. I started thinking about the fact
that there was very little known about the use of electrical communication among cells and electrical
signaling. And it seemed to me that one of the best examples of systems that made decisions and
stored memories and created self-models and have all kinds of these complex functions is the brain
and nervous system. And of course, the brain and nervous system do exactly what a lot of our
technology does, which is it capitalizes on how good electrical signaling is for processing
information and for computation. And it seemed impossible that evolution wouldn't have discovered
that long before brains showed up on the evolutionary scene. So I was always interested in the role of
electricity and in particular bioelectricity in these kinds of problems. But I didn't talk about it much
because I wanted to get a grounding in sort of mainstream cell biology. But then once I was on
my own in my own lab at Forsyth, then I left the Sunroll. So that's what we've been doing for the last
20 years is studying the whole set of questions. Very cool. Well, Mike, thanks so much for sharing
your journey. And you mentioned something that I'm fascinated by, that you and your dad started this
software company relatively early on in your career. And I'm curious how you made that decision to move
back towards academia as opposed to maybe pursuing an industry or entrepreneurship route.
It was a really tough decision. In fact, it was a series of those decisions that at first,
I wasn't even sure I was going to go to college. I was having great fun doing programming. I was
making money. It seemed like everything was pretty much fine as it is. But then just to do the sort of
bigger things in AI and so on, I did want a science degree. At that point, we had this company and it
was a pretty tough choice because I was really hooked on science and on research. But it never quite seemed to
me like having my own lab and being in charge of investigating these problems, it never quite seemed
realistic to me. Actually, for years, I kind of had this feeling in the back of my head that this
is quite temporary and that I'd be in some way kicked out or washed out. And then at that point,
I would just go back and do more coding. So my strategy was to simply see how far I could get.
I would just keep doing what I was doing. And at some point, if it ended, it ended. But I really had
no sort of clear expectation that this was going to work out like this. But by the time that I applied
and actually got into grad school, then it certainly seemed like I needed to see that through and see how
that went. So fairly reluctantly, we left the company and I pursued the academic realm.
Gotcha. And I really love that you brought up this idea that it didn't almost seem real, this opportunity
that you had or the possibility that you could be successful in science. And I think that's something
that a lot of young scientists struggle with. So when did it really feel real for you? Or when did you feel
like this was something that you could make happen?
Right around 2007, when I got tenure.
Yeah.
I'm not even kidding, because up until then, pretty much everything is always kind of hanging
on a thread, right? It's always, well, what have you published lately? And where's your next grant
coming from? And this kind of thing. And especially for me, having come from a different field and not
having had the same in-depth biochemistry and genetics background, graduate school was very tough
for me because I didn't have the same background that a lot of the other students had. All of that just
made it seem like this was one massive experiment. It was entirely unclear how any of this was going to work
out. And also because I knew that I was fundamentally interested in pursuing very out-of-the-box
research topics. And these are high-risk, kind of high-reward things. You never know how they're
going to turn out. So it always seemed like we'll find out how it goes.
Right. Well, Mike, I'm so glad that you persisted and you stuck it out in this long experiment because
you have so many cool research projects going on right now. And it's going to be hard to choose,
but I'm going to ask you today, is there one that you want to tell us a little bit more about that
you are the most excited to be working on? Well, there are many. And all of the things
in my lab are focused fundamentally on understanding how cells and tissues make group decisions and how
they cooperate together to make and repair large-scale structures that we see during
development and regeneration. One of the projects that I guess we can talk about is a very recent one
on the role of the very early brain in patterning the body. And one of the main questions in this whole
field is where does the information for the anatomy come from? So every normal embryo has
the same complex anatomical layout. But of course, the genome specifies proteins. It doesn't directly
say how many eyes you're going to have, how many fingers, or in fact, if you'll have fingers or any
of that. So one big question is where does this information come from? And one of the things that
we discovered recently, and this is just something that was published a couple months ago in Nature
Communications, was it turns out that part of that information comes from the very early brain.
And when I say very early, this is two days of development in the frog embryo. So this is long
before behavior. There's no muscle movement. The embryo is not moving around. In fact, there are no
muscles yet. This is incredibly early. And one of the first things the brain does, as it turns out,
while it itself is still being put together, the brain is nowhere near even finished being assembled.
But one of the first things it does is it spreads information throughout the whole animal,
throughout the whole body that helps pattern everything from the muscles, from the peripheral nerve
system. Lots of aspects of development actually depend on the brain. And it turns out that if
that brain isn't there, or if it's suppressed in some way, then all sorts of things go wrong. And in
particular, influences such as various drugs, which normally have no effect on embryonic development,
without proper influence from the brain, they become potent teratogens. So it turns out that the early
brain is actually protecting embryos from teratogenesis by constantly putting out these patterning signals
that help the other structures know what they should be doing. And in fact, it also turns out from work
we did a couple of years ago, that the reverse is also true, that the early brain, in terms of knowing
how large to grow and what shape to make, is also getting cues from the rest of the body as far away
as the belly and other regions of the body. So it's this massive loop between the neural and
non-neural tissues that enable both of them to form properly during development. And this is a super
exciting process. It's a project that is spearheaded in my group by a very talented postdoc,
Celia Herrera-Rincon is her name. And she published some very nice work on this. And we're just now
beginning to mine the implications of this for understanding teratogenesis, for understanding
why certain drugs and other influences harm some embryos and not others, what the role of the brain
is in this process, and how we can exploit these signals to actually improve the situation in case of
birth defects, and even regeneration from injury. That's just one of the most recent stories we've
had.
Certainly. And I think it's so fascinating that the work that you're doing, like you just mentioned,
goes all the way from development, but it continues going on through adulthood. And in some organisms,
particularly where regenesis of whole body parts or things like that are happening, this is something
that persists throughout their whole life, this ability for different parts of the body,
different cells to be communicating, to organize or reorganize that structure, which I think is amazing.
Absolutely. And it's crucial to think about it through lifespan, because there are situations
in which individual cells of the body sort of defect from that overall plan, and this is known
as cancer. So there are a set of cues and communication signals that cells send to each other to enable
them to cooperate together towards maintaining anatomical structures during adulthood. But sometimes
that process breaks down. And when it breaks down and cells don't receive signals from the rest of the
body, they sort of revert back to their unicellular evolutionary past, and they go off on their own,
and they treat the rest of the body as just part of the environment, and they do whatever they want
to do, which is to reproduce and go where they want. So this ends up as carcinogenesis and metastasis.
So we also have projects in the lab where we've looked at how electrical signaling is keeping cells
harnessed to this body plant, and how breakdown in that process can induce malignancy, even in the
absence of, let's say, genetic defects or carcinogens or mutations or any of that.
So like you said, this is very important all the way from early development, all the way through
adulthood.
Well, this is an incredible project, Mike, and I'm so glad you shared it with us today. And of course,
congratulations on this recent Nature Communications paper. And I think thus far,
we've talked about a lot of great aspects of your career and how you got to where you are today. And
we've touched just a little bit on some of the challenges and the struggles. And I think these are
so important to talk about in science, because they don't often see the light of day. But do you have a
favorite challenge or a struggle or a failure that you've experienced at some point in your career
that you want to tell our listeners about and give them some insight into how you work through this
tough time?
Well, there have been many. I guess first, I'll just talk about one specific event that happened.
And this was back when I was a postdoc, and I was studying left-right patterning. So the question of
how the cells on the left and right side of your body know which side they're on so that they can direct
the patterning of the asymmetric organs like the heart, the liver, and so on appropriately. This was
work done in frog embryos. One of the ways that we do this work is we take embryos and we do various
things to them to test our theories. And then we wait and let them develop for about a week. And then
we look at the various organs. So we look at where the heart ended up, where the gut ended up,
and we check to see if they're on the correct side or not. So comparing a set of treated embryos
where some of the organs may be on the wrong side has to be done relative to controls where
under normal circumstances, all the organs are on their correct side. So we went through about four
months in the middle of this project where many of my control embryos, completely normal embryos to
which nothing was done, suddenly all the organs were randomized. And this is a condition called
heterotaxia, which also happens in human birth defects, where each organ basically makes an
independent decision about what side it's going to go to. And you can imagine it's very problematic
for the embryo because things don't fit together. Yeah, they don't fit together. But the problem here
was that the controls were doing this. So you would see 20 to 30% of control embryos have their organs
on the wrong side. And the problem with that is that it made it completely impossible to interpret
any other effects you might have induced when your controls are already as a baseline,
a third of them is already randomized. This was a horror. And it went on for months,
and it just basically made it impossible to get any data during this time. And it was driving me
completely insane. And that's the sort of thing that can be really demotivating because you're
cruising along, you're getting data, you've got things that are working, you've got deadlines,
you've got papers that take a while, you've got conferences you need to present at,
and suddenly you can't do a good experiment because your controls are all messed up.
And very few people actually study left-right patterning. Nobody was studying the kinds of
processes that we were studying. So the physiology and the biophysics of it, there was really nobody
to talk to about this problem. And it was driving me insane. And what I was doing was trying to figure
out what it could possibly be that was causing this. And what it turned out to be eventually was that
we raised the animals in this medium called MMR. It's basically like a very low salt water solution.
It just basically pulled like spring water almost. And it turned out that the MMR that we were using
for our embryos, we had a new technician that started in the lab and he wasn't pH-ing it properly.
And it was at a very low pH. Now, nobody else had noticed this because drops in pH don't really
affect much of anything in embryogenesis, at least for the frog, that anybody could tell.
But it turned out that it was absolutely crucial for left-right patterning. And as soon as I found out
that the pH was off, all the pieces clicked into place. Because what we had discovered then was that
one of the very important early steps for figuring out which side is left and which side is right
is to drive an asymmetric proton gradient. There were these proton pumps that were on the right
side of the animal that would provide this gradient. And having an aberrant pH in the
surrounding medium was basically inhibiting their ability to do this. So this was actually a good
experiment on its own. And then we ended up doing some very careful control conditions with specific
pHs and so on. And then everything snapped into place. But until then, it was sort of quite demotivating.
And I think a lot of people go through periods where just technically things stop working for
mysterious reasons. And biology is very complicated. It's much harder than, let's say,
computer science, where you can really debug very cleanly. You might have a mess of code and you
might know that there's a problem somewhere. But you're pretty much guaranteed that if you sit
there long enough and you step through it step by step, you're going to find the error.
Right. And it behaves the same every time, right?
Yes. Mostly it behaves the same way every time. So you have a pretty good chance that you're going to
find whatever the issue is. Biology is like that. Often everybody who's been in the lab knows that
you see these things and say, why in the world is that happening? And then it never shows up again,
or it comes and it goes. And we just don't know all the factors that go into it. So that's the
kind of thing that can be super frustrating.
Well, I love this story of serendipitous discovery. And I'm really glad to hear that
you didn't abandon it. I think so often things don't work out as they expect and you sort of ignore
the weird results and move on to something else. But I think really digging into those weird results
and trying to figure out what happened can lead to some really fascinating results.
Absolutely.
Well, great story of a challenge. And I'm so glad you walked us through how you worked through it,
because I think these are some of the struggles that our listeners out there are going to face
in their own careers as scientists. And it can be frustrating to not get data for months and really
be banging your head against the wall to get this experiment to work. But that's not the end of
the line there. There can be a light at the end of the tunnel. And I think that's a great message to
share with our listeners who might be going through some of these struggles themselves.
But we don't just want to talk about the struggles, Mike. I'd love for you next to share one of your
success stories with our listeners, whether it's a big success or a small one.
Well, another recent success that I'm very proud of is a work by now a staff scientist in our center,
Bifov Pi, and our collaborator, Alexis Pytak. They did some very interesting work on trying to
understand how the brain is patterned, the early brain. This is also a story in frog. And in particular,
this is a success story of involving computational modeling. And a lot of computational models are a
long way away from practical applications. Sometimes you make these mathematical models,
and it's not quite clear what you can do with them. So this is an example of one that turned out to be
really a practical use of what they were able to do was to create a model in which we really try to
understand the electrical properties of all the cells that are going to eventually give rise to the brain.
And in making this model, they were able to understand why it is that certain drugs,
things like alcohol and nicotine, really perturbed that pattern and thus result in birth defects.
And they were able to use that model to ask a simple question. In the case of this kind of
teratogenic influence, what would you have to do in order to fix it? And remarkably, and this is just
the whole chain from asking the question, coming up with a computational model that explains
the physiology data that you see, and then inverting that model to ask, what can you do to correct a
pathological condition? And then actually testing those suggestions in the lab, they were able to,
this model actually suggests a very specific treatment that when we tried it, in fact,
fixed the defects, despite the fact that these embryos have been treated with these really nasty
compounds. And these animals got their brain shape back, they got their gene expression back
appropriately in the brain, and they got their IQs back. So it was incredible to see that this model
was actually making predictions that were therapeutically efficacious. And that just blew
me away. And I still think that this is one of our great successes.
Well, that is remarkable, Mike. And now you've captivated my curiosity here. So I'm curious,
in this situation where you're exposing the embryo to a noxious substance, do you have to
intervene or fix it immediately? Or can there be a time lag?
That is a very good question. That is what we're investigating now. So a couple of things we're
doing now is checking the timing. So how late can you intervene? That's actually a really
interesting question that depends on your perspective. So for example, in our regenerative
